Neonatal ringtails (Bassariscus astutus) are remarkably diminutive, with newborns weighing approximately 30 grams [Wwb = approximately 30 grams] at a body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], a value that underscores their altricial condition. This modest birth mass, typical of carnivorans that give birth to litters of altricial young and consistent with other members of the family Procyonidae, is followed by a relatively rapid phase of maternal investment. Females aggressively defend their dens, typically rocky crevices or hollow trees, and provide exclusive maternal care during the initial weeks post-partum. The growth trajectory from this neonatal stage to nutritional independence is steep, reflecting the high energetic demands of the suckling juvenile. Weaning, marking the cessation of lactation and the transition to solid food, is documented to occur at 42 days following birth [tx = 42 days following birth] under the same thermal conditions, a point at which the young have nearly decupled their mass at a temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C]. This weaning age aligns closely with the timing of first solid food ingestion observed in captive colonies, where juveniles begin accepting invertebrate prey offered by the mother shortly before the fourth week of life. The rapid mass gain during this pre-weaning interval is critical for the subsequent survival of the young as they transition to independent foraging in the complex arboreal habitats this species favors across its southwestern North American range.

Gestation in the ringtail lasts 52 days [tg = 52 days] at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], a relatively short period for a carnivoran of this body size that reflects the altricial state of the neonates at parturition. This gestation period is comparable to that of other procyonids such as the white-nosed coati (Nasua narica) and the kinkajou (Potos flavus), though ringtails tend to produce slightly smaller litters. The timing of the mating season, typically in late winter to early spring, ensures that births coincide with the peak availability of insect and small vertebrate prey, which is critical for the lactating female to meet the high energetic demands of milk production. Following birth, the female remains in the den with her litter almost continuously for the first several weeks, emerging only briefly to forage. This intensive maternal care strategy is essential for the survival of the altricial neonates, which are born with closed eyes and limited thermoregulatory capacity.

Sexual maturity in ringtails is reached at 300 days after birth [tp = 300 days after birth] when maintained at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], a relatively early age compared to many other procyonids. This rapid onset of reproductive capability allows individuals born early in the year to potentially breed in their first spring, contributing to the species' capacity for population recovery following periods of low density. The attainment of sexual maturity coincides with the completion of skeletal growth and the acquisition of adult-like foraging skills. Adult ringtails achieve an ultimate asymptotic body weight of 1015 grams [Wwi = 1015 grams] under the same thermal conditions, a mass that places them among the smaller members of the family Procyonidae. This adult body mass, combined with their slender build and long tail, is an adaptation for their scansorial lifestyle, allowing them to navigate complex arboreal environments efficiently in pursuit of prey and to escape larger predators.

Reproduction in the ringtail is characterized by a single annual litter, with females producing one clutch per year in spring [F_R_i = one clutch per year in spring]. Litter sizes typically range from one to four pups, with an average of approximately three offspring per litter [N_R_i = approximately three offspring per litter]. This annual reproductive output, typical of many small to medium-sized carnivorans, reflects a trade-off between current reproductive investment and the maintenance of maternal body condition for future breeding seasons. The timing of reproduction is tightly linked to seasonal resource availability, with peak lactation coinciding with the spring pulse of insect and small vertebrate prey. The maximum lifespan of the ringtail reaches 19 years [am = 19 years] when kept at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], with some captive individuals documented to survive even longer under optimal conditions. This longevity is remarkable for a mammal of this size and is likely linked to their relatively low metabolic rate, which may reduce oxidative damage and slow the rate of cellular aging.

Weaning weight in the ringtail is approximately 258.7 grams [Wwx = approximately 258.7 grams] when measured at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], representing nearly an order of magnitude increase from the birth weight of 30 grams [Wwb = 30 grams] over the 42-day nursing period. This rapid growth rate is supported by the high fat and protein content of ringtail milk, which is among the richest reported for procyonids. The weaning weight is a critical determinant of juvenile survival, as heavier individuals are better able to compete for food resources and are less susceptible to predation during the vulnerable post-weaning period. After weaning, juveniles continue to associate with their mother for several weeks, learning foraging techniques and developing the arboreal agility necessary for independent survival. The combination of a relatively short gestation, rapid postnatal growth, and early sexual maturity allows ringtail populations to respond quickly to favorable environmental conditions, though their strict dependence on high-quality maternal care limits population growth in years of low resource availability.
